title: Marguerite and the Asset
premise: Coral Dunmore, a crash investigator whose family died in row twelve of Flight 4471, has spent five years in witness protection guarding a defector known only as the Asset — a man whose testimony about the crash keeps shifting. When the safe house appears on a real estate listing with interior photos, Coral realizes someone inside the program is selling them out, and that the Asset may be bait in a larger trade. Racing to move him before the border checkpoint shifts change, Coral uncovers that her own memories of row twelve were surgically altered to protect the real informant. In the end, Coral chooses truth over loyalty: she exposes the program, lets the Asset face justice at the border, and finally remembers what actually happened in row twelve.
about_author: I. M. Sandoval is the pen name of a former aviation safety analyst who spent a decade reviewing black-box transcripts before turning to fiction. They write from a coastal town they are not permitted to name.

chapters.title: Row Twelve
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Five years after the crash, Coral reviews wreckage photos she can barely look at, then drives to the safe house where the Asset waits behind blackout curtains. The emotional beat is grief held at arm's length by procedure; she recites protocol like a prayer to avoid remembering her family's seat numbers.

chapters.title: The Listing
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. A routine sweep finds the safe house on a real estate site — twelve interior photos, timestamps from last week. The handler, Voss, insists it's a glitch. Coral notices a coffee mug in frame three that belongs to no one on the protection roster. The beat is dread arriving through something as mundane as a listing photo.

chapters.title: The Asset's Version
chapters.summary: Asset's POV (unnamed). He rehearses his testimony again, noticing it has changed in small ways he can't account for — dates, a cargo manifest, a name. He suspects Coral is being managed as much as he is. The beat is paranoia curdling into pity for the woman guarding him.

chapters.title: Protocol Revision Seven
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. New rules arrive: no phone, no vehicle, movement window cut to ninety minutes. Voss claims it's standard. Coral maps the revisions against the listing date and finds every rule change followed an information leak. Beat: the slow horror of realizing the cage was built around her, not the Asset.

chapters.title: What Coral Remembers
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, interleaved with fragmented memory. She tries to reconstruct the funeral, the identification, the call — and finds gaps with clean edges, like edited tape. She visits the crash archive and discovers her own witness statement was filed twice, with different wording. Beat: grief turning suspicious of itself.

chapters.title: The Buyer's Agent
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Posing as a buyer, she contacts the listing agent and traces the photos to a staging company paid through a shell tied to the program's own budget line. Someone inside funded the exposure. Beat: cold competence masking rising fear; she tells no one what she found.

chapters.title: Ninety Minutes
chapters.summary: Asset's POV. During a supply run window, he tests Coral — mentions a detail about the crash only a passenger would know. Her reaction isn't confusion but recognition she immediately suppresses. He concludes she was on the plane or connected to it. Beat: the guarded beginning of an alliance neither trusts.

chapters.title: Voss's Quiet Call
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss reports to an unnamed superior that Coral is 'asking about row twelve' and requests authorization for 'the next revision.' We learn the Asset's extraction is scheduled to fail. Beat: institutional menace — bureaucracy as violence, conducted in calm voices over secure lines.

chapters.title: The Altered Statement
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She breaks into the records annex and compares her two statements: one says she saw a maintenance truck on the tarmac; the other doesn't. The second copy bears her signature dated a day she has no memory of. Beat: vertigo — the past itself becomes unreliable terrain.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Rotation
chapters.summary: Asset's POV. He memorizes the border checkpoint shift schedule hidden in his own debrief notes and realizes the extraction route crosses during the one shift change when surveillance doubles. Either his handlers are incompetent or he is meant to be caught. Beat: resignation hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Two Truths in a Kitchen
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Over burnt coffee, Coral and the Asset trade what they know: her edited memory, his drifting testimony. They agree the crash story was rewritten to protect whoever put the maintenance truck there. Beat: wary intimacy — two people deciding, almost simultaneously, to stop obeying.

chapters.title: Revision Eight
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The new protocol orders her to sedate the Asset for transport — medically unnecessary, procedurally unprecedented. She signs the acknowledgment form with a steady hand while planning to disobey it. Beat: the quiet moment loyalty officially dies.

chapters.title: The Staging House
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She tracks the staging company to a warehouse and finds furniture replicas of the safe house — and a full-scale mockup of an aircraft cabin, rows marked, row twelve dressed with personal effects including her mother's scarf. Beat: the thriller's conspiracy acquires a physical, intimate body; Coral nearly breaks.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, fragmentary. Under stress, the blocked memory surfaces: she wasn't just a bereaved relative — she was a junior investigator who photographed the maintenance truck the night before the crash, and the program erased the night to bury the photo. Beat: devastating reorientation; survival itself becomes evidence.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss confronts Coral gently, offering reinstatement, her real memories restored, if she delivers the Asset sedated as ordered. He implies her family's deaths were partly her photograph's fault. Beat: temptation weaponized through guilt; Coral asks for one night to decide.

chapters.title: Running the Window
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Coral fakes the sedation, and they slip out during the ninety-minute window, using the real estate photos' timestamps to predict the surveillance rotation. A tail spots them at a fuel stop. Beat: kinetic escape sequence powered entirely by earlier planted details.

chapters.title: The Man Who Sold the House
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Cornered, they confront the staging coordinator, who confesses: the listing was deliberate bait to flush the Asset toward the checkpoint, where a foreign service would take him in exchange for burying the crash file — and Coral's photograph. Beat: the trap's full shape revealed; the enemy wanted them running.

chapters.title: Diversion at Mile Forty
chapters.summary: Asset's POV. The Asset volunteers to be seen taking a decoy route, buying Coral time to reach the archive copy of her original photo. His goodbye is understated — he calls her by her real name for the first time. Beat: sacrifice offered freely, redeeming five years of lies.

chapters.title: Shift Change
chapters.summary: Dual POV. At the border, the Asset walks into the doubled shift exactly as planned — but Coral, having broadcast the original maintenance-truck photo to three news desks minutes earlier, forces both governments to take him alive rather than let him vanish. Beat: climax; truth deployed as a weapon sharper than any extraction plan.

chapters.title: Row Twelve, Remembered
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. With the file public, Coral's unaltered memory returns whole: her family died because the truck's work failed, not because of her photo — the guilt was installed to control her. She grieves them for the first time honestly. Beat: catharsis; memory reclaimed is not comfort, but it is hers.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Months later, she testifies at the hearing, watching the Asset — named now, human — give the testimony he could never safely give before. Voss is indicted; the program is dismantled. Beat: justice rendered imperfectly but publicly; loyalty to institutions replaced by loyalty to fact.

chapters.title: The House That Sold
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral buys the safe house at auction, strips the blackout curtains, and lets the light in. On the last page she pins the real estate photo to the wall — proof that invisibility was never safety, and that being seen is survivable. Beat: quiet resolution; the survivor stops hiding and starts living.
